## Tidy Scripting

I told you that there would be less typing under the tidyverse, but it feels like we have been doing a very similar amount!

### dplyr
The package 'dplyr' is going to help us reduce the amount of typing we have to do.

`dplyr` provides a set of _verbs_ (aka functions) that can be used to manipulate dataframes.
All dplyr verbs have the following in common:

- First argument is always a dataframe,
- Subsequent arguments refer to the columns of the dataframe to be acted on
- The output is always a dataframe.

Another feature that's going to help us minimise typing is the pipe operator.
The pipe has a couple of forms:

- %>%
- |>

We're going to use the second one as it is newer - but note that the first one has it's uses (they are not identical).


The pipe feeds the output from one function to the input of another.
In common language you could replace the pipe with 'and then'.

So:-

```{R, eval=FALSE}

df |>
  my_function() |>
  my_other_function |>
  print()

```

Is essentially saying:

"start with df and then do my function to it, and then do my other function to the output, and then print the final output"

The tidyverse is written in such a way that it is as easy to read a script as it is to read the above sentence.


### Summarising data

We're going to explore tidy scripting using a personality dataset.

Load this using `load('data/big_five.rds')`.

This loads an object called `bfi` into the environment.

Lets have a look at the columns.
We're going to use `glimpse()` again, but this time with a pipe:

```{R, eval=FALSE}

bfi |>
  glimpse()

```

Next, we're going to calculate the mean agreeableness score between males and females in this dataset.

```{R, eval=FALSE}
bfi |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarise(average_agreeableness=mean(agree, na.rm=TRUE))
```

The above does the following:

- Calls up the bfi dataframe
- Groups it by gender
- Calculates the mean and returns the output as a dataframe.

#### Exercise
Repeat the above with the other personality traits.

### Selecting

Rather than working with a whole dataframe, we can extract a subset of columns using the `select()` verb.
The select verb can take either column names, or a search function.

#### Column name

```{R, eval=FALSE}
bfi |>
  select(agree) %>%
  summarise(average_agreeableness=mean(agree, na.rm=TRUE))
```

#### Search function

```{R, eval=FALSE}
bfi |>
  select(starts_with('a')) %>%
  summarise(average_agreeableness=mean(agree, na.rm=TRUE), age=mean(age))
```


  
### Filtering

We might also want to only look at participants from a particular subgroup.
For instance, let's look at people who are currently in high school.
We can use the 'filter' verb to do this.

```{R, eval=FALSE}
bfi |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  filter(education=='high_school') |>
  summarise(average_agreeableness=mean(agree, na.rm=TRUE))
```

Do we get a different value?

#### Exercise

Try filtering by other categories.


### dplyr and ggplot

As ggplot is part of the tidyverse, it works seamlessly with `dplyr`.

```{R, eval=FALSE}
bfi |>
  filter(education=='high_school') |>
  ggplot(aes(y=agree, x=age)) +
  geom_point()
```

For the rest of the session, you will be exploring the datasets using what we have learned about visualisation and scripting.

Using any of the datasets that we have used today, come up with some exploratory research questions and create a plot that will answer this.

Are two particular personality traits likely to be correlated?
Might this relationship vary between genders, or between people from different educational backgrounds?

Feel free to revisit the stroop dataset or the penguin dataset, or the sleep dataset from last week.

I will be around to help you formulate a research question and answer any questions about how to develop your plot using R.
